segments_en: And one who stirs. See Taz in siman 318, seif katan 22 and 23. With wool, either the reason is that it requires extensive cooking, which appears to be the Mechaber's view here and will, with God's help, be explained below in Magen Avraham, seif katan 2, or the prohibition is dyeing. See the Rosh at the beginning of Shabbos, daf 18b, who cites Rashi's explanation that stirring constitutes cooking. In the chapter Kirah, daf 40b, siman 11, the Rosh cites two explanations. One is that stirring constitutes cooking, for although there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking, dyes used for coloring continually require further cooking. Alternatively, stirring constitutes dyeing because through stirring the dyes enter the wool. This is what the Taz means in siman 318, seif katan 22, when he writes that wool requires extensive cooking. More precisely, it is the dyes that require extensive cooking, and cooking after cooking continues to apply to them. A practical difference arises where one stirs a vat of dyes containing no wool, etc. This will, with God's help, be explained in siman 318 and here in Magen Avraham, seif katan 2. The author says: I considered it appropriate to write here several specific points concerning this matter. Rashi on Shabbos, daf 18b, s.v.
The Rambam, of blessed memory, writes in chapter 3, halacha 11 of Hilchos Shabbos:

I will add one further point. Hagahos Maimoniyos, chapter 3, seif katan 6, disagrees with Sefer HaTerumah concerning food that is fully cooked. Some explain that Rabbeinu Chananel is discussing fully cooked food, and that inserting the ladle is itself actual stirring. Accordingly, even fully cooked food is forbidden to stir while on the fire, either by Torah law because, although there is no prohibition of cooking after cooking, stirring advances the cooking further, or at least by rabbinic law. The Rambam's wording,

There remains another matter to clarify. There are three possible reasons to prohibit stirring a dye vat after it has been removed from the fire. The first is cooking, as Rashi explains and as the Rosh writes in the chapter Kirah, daf 40b, siman 11, and as the Bach explains in siman 318, because dyes continually require further cooking. According to this, the prohibition applies specifically in a kli rishon while it is yad soledes bo. The second is the Rosh's second explanation, namely dyeing: by stirring, the dyes enter the wool. Each explanation apparently produces both a leniency and a stringency. According to the first explanation, there is a leniency in a kli sheni or when it is not yad soledes bo, but a stringency even after the wool has already absorbed the color before Shabbos, because the dyes still continually require cooking. According to the second explanation, there is a leniency if the wool already absorbed the color before Shabbos, since dyeing no longer applies, but a stringency in that even in a kli sheni one can say that stirring causes dyeing. I learned a third reason from the Ran on Shabbos: it is the normal practice of dyers to stir so that the wool does not scorch. This also appears from the Jerusalem Talmud. It seems that this reason too is part of the melacha of dyeing, because preventing the wool from scorching is part of the dyeing process. Accordingly, even after it has absorbed the color it remains forbidden. In a kli sheni, however, one can say that scorching does not apply and it is permitted, perhaps even where the wool has not yet absorbed the color. Thus each explanation has its own leniency and stringency. With God's help, this will be explained in Magen Avraham, seif katan 2.

segments_en: If it is beer. See Taz. His difficulty is based on an unnecessary blessing. Regarding precedence, however, even HaMotzi precedes Borei Peri HaGefen, as explained in siman 211, seif 5. Nevertheless, one can say that for Kiddush wine has special importance and therefore comes first, whereas with respect to an unnecessary blessing, etc. He answers that the blessing is unavoidable, because bread exempts all beverages. One can say that their practice was to drink wine before the meal to stimulate the appetite. His question, however, concerns only beer, etc. What he wrote, that one should intend not to exempt the bread, is difficult. In siman 206, seif 2, the Mechaber rules that only where one specifically intended does one item exempt another, whereas without intent it does not. All the more so, beer should not exempt bread, for even with items of equal status intent is required. Moreover, the flow of his language implies that the reason one should intend not to exempt the bread is so that it will be evident that the Shehakol is being recited for Kiddush. If he intended the Shehakol to exempt the bread, it would no longer be evident that he recited Shehakol because of Kiddush. But even without this consideration, l'chatchila each item requires its appropriate blessing. See Magen Avraham, siman 206, seif katan 2, and the Gemara, where the alternative blessing is effective only b'dieved.

Know that the daytime Kiddush is d'rabbanan, yet women are obligated in it. As Magen Avraham wrote in siman 291, seif katan 11, regarding all matters of Shabbos, men and women are equal even in rabbinic matters. Whoever is included in rabbinic observance of Shabbos, including muktzeh and shevus prohibitions, is likewise included in remembering Shabbos through the daytime Kiddush. See siman 597, Magen Avraham, seif katan 3. One who fasts on Shabbos does not recite the rabbinic Kiddusha Rabbah in the morning, but at night, when Kiddush is by Torah law, one can say that he must recite Kiddush. We wrote about this in Peri Chadash. Regarding whether one who does not himself drink may recite Borei Peri HaGefen in the morning to discharge others, see siman 273, Taz, seif katan 3, and siman 167, seif 7, Magen Avraham there. Beit Yosef there cites two opinions concerning Borei Peri HaGefen of the morning Kiddush; see there. At first glance, since daytime Kiddush was instituted because of oneg Shabbos, perhaps it resembles the rule in siman 205 that one cannot discharge others, or perhaps there is not such a significant difference. See Magen Avraham and Taz there in siman 167. This still requires further study. The Rama in siman 273, seif 4, rules that one may discharge others in the morning.

What the Mechaber wrote concerning a prepared bed applies to one whose practice is to sit upon a prepared bed. According to our practice, if the bed is in the room where one eats, he should arrange it in the morning. See Magen Avraham, siman 302, seif katan 6, and see the Prisha and Shiyarei Knesset HaGedolah regarding this.

If in the morning he has no wine and has only bread, so that he may not eat other foods before reciting HaMotzi, as Magen Avraham wrote in seif katan 4, one can say that he may recite HaMotzi to discharge others even though he does not eat with them. See siman 273, Taz, seif katan 3, and Magen Avraham, siman 167, seif katan 1. According to the Taz there, seif katan 17, however, he cannot discharge them because there is no distinguishing feature.

segments_en: Seif katan 2. Three men, etc., because there is nothing here with which to make an interruption, etc. After U'va LeTzion they recite Kaddish, and after the Torah reading, before Shemoneh Esrei, they likewise recite Kaddish. If Kaddish were recited at the bimah after the Torah reading, how could they again recite Kaddish before Shemoneh Esrei when there is no intervening matter between the two Kaddishim? Granted, at Shacharis there is an interruption between the two Kaddishim, namely Ashrei, which is recited after the Kaddish following the Torah reading. At Minchah, however, Ashrei has already been recited before the Torah reading, and nothing is recited afterward. Even on a fast day at Minchah one might have thought that Kaddish should be recited after three men have read from the Torah, before the haftarah, so that the haftarah would constitute an interruption between the two Kaddishim. Magen Avraham therefore writes that the haftarah belongs to the Torah reading and is covered by the Kaddish recited before the haftarah. If so, what purpose would the Kaddish before Shemoneh Esrei serve?

Rivash writes, etc., that in a place where there is no Sefer Torah, the Kaddish before Shemoneh Esrei is not recited. They already recited Kaddish after U'va LeTzion, so upon what would the second Kaddish be recited? Eliyah Rabbah asks that according to what Magen Avraham wrote at the end of siman 143, even in a place without a Sefer Torah the chazzan should read aloud from a Chumash. If so, the reading from the Chumash should constitute an interruption. Tevuos Shor likewise writes:
They should likewise not recite Va'ani Sefilasi, as written above in the preceding seif katan according to the reason stated there.

One might say that they should recite Va'ani Sefilasi and then recite Kaddish upon it. Meaning, according to the second reason, namely that there should not be an interruption, etc., there is a solution: after Va'ani Sefilasi they could recite another Kaddish.

From the statement concerning Yehallelu. Meaning, regarding what was written above, that for this reason Kaddish is not recited at Minchah after the Torah reading because there is nothing to interrupt between the Kaddish following the reading and the Kaddish before Shemoneh Esrei, there is seemingly an interruption through recitation of Yehallelu when the Sefer Torah is returned to the aron. Rather, it must be that a single verse is not considered an interruption.

Or they should recite it, etc. Meaning, if they nevertheless wish to recite Va'ani Sefilasi, they should recite it immediately after completing U'va LeTzion and then recite Kaddish afterward, so there will be no interruption. Nevertheless, according to the reason stated above in seif katan 1, it should not be recited even immediately after completing U'va LeTzion.

segments_en: It is permitted. See Rivash, cited by the Beit Yosef, who permits it for several reasons and concludes: all the more so in this case, where the non-Jew was not found beside the wine or inside the storeroom, we need not believe him that either he or another person entered there. See below, siman 130, at the end of seif 8 in the Rama's gloss, that if a barrel of wine was in the possession of a non-Jew and he says it was dripping, that he repaired it, and that he touched the wine, he is not believed. See Responsa Maharil, siman 38.

Because the non-Jewish woman is not believed. But if it is known that she took wine from the cellar, it is forbidden. This follows the law of the Gemara. Alternatively, the case may be one where she cannot take the wine without touching it with her hand, such as where there is no spigot in the barrel and she must draw wine by hand from the barrel or vat. Although even in such a case it is possible for her to avoid touching the wine, for example by drawing it with a vessel and carefully avoiding all contact with her hand, nevertheless we are concerned that she may have touched it incidentally while occupied with the task, as above in siman 128, seif 4, in the Rama's gloss. Where there is a spigot, however, so that her hand itself did not touch the wine in the barrel and she acted only through the spigot, then even if it is known that she took wine from the cellar, according to us nowadays it is permitted in a case of loss. This is because it is contact by a non-Jew through another object without intent, as explained above in siman 124 and below in the following seif katan.

Siman 125. This is the reading in the books and in Olat Tamid, and so it appears in Darkei Moshe. I do not know what relevance that siman has here. It appears to be an error, and the text should read siman 124, or perhaps siman 128. The meaning would then be that in seif 4 there it was explained that we are not concerned that a non-Jew touched wine for the purpose of idolatrous libation unless he touched it for his own benefit. Since contemporary non-Jews do not pour wine for idolatrous libation, here too we are not concerned that the woman deliberately touched it with her hand for that purpose. In siman 124, seif 24, it was explained that nowadays, since non-Jews are not idolaters, even if she deliberately removed the spigot it is permitted, because since her intent was not idolatrous libation it is contact by a non-Jew through another object without intent. The same applies here. We are not concerned that she touched the wine in the barrel itself with her hand, or that she touched the wine that flowed outside when she drew it, which would cause the wine inside to become forbidden through nitzok, because she has no need to do so. This is also explicit in the Mordechai there. At the conclusion of the incident concerning one who hid the key, cited above, he writes:

segments_en: Vessels of neser, etc. Tosafos in Avodah Zarah, daf 33b, wrote that there are two kinds of neser. This kind is not the one mentioned in the first chapter of Shabbos, where it states that vessels of neser and earthenware vessels have the same law of impurity. There is also a third kind of neser from which vessels are not made, but which is used for laundering vessels. See there.

From a quarry of tzerif, which is called alum. See Taz and Prisha. Rivash, siman 450, and the Bartenura at the beginning of chapter 2 of Keilim likewise write that this is what is called alum. Rambam there, however, extensively refutes those who say so and explains that it is the substance called tafel in Arabic. See below, siman 159, seif 2.

segments_en: He ages them. The knots must be untied, as I will write shortly.

Rinsing suffices for them. This implies rinsing with cold water, and so it appears in Hagahos Ashri and the Mordechai there. They write, however, that this applies specifically to laundering in which the practice is to beat the cloth several times. Tosafos likewise writes this. From the Rosh, however, it appears that it is permitted only with the type of laundering in which the practice is to wash several times with ashes, then with hot water in a kli sheni, and then with cold water. It appears that they do not disagree, because Tosafos, Mordechai, and Hagahos Ashri conclude that it requires further study whether, regarding prohibitions, one should distinguish between a substance that adheres and one that does not adhere. The Rosh there explains why all tablecloths upon which a hot prohibition fell are permitted even where the prohibited substance adheres, because in such a case laundering specifically with hot water and ashes is required. So it appears to me.

notes: Fresh translation of both Hebrew slots.
segments_en: It is permitted to lend, etc. What difference does it make that the collateral does not belong to the non-Jew? Is it forbidden to lend money to a non-Jew upon collateral belonging to a Jew? Even if the non-Jew had lent money to the first Jew with interest, it is permitted for a second Jew to lend money with interest to the non-Jew upon that same collateral and to receive from the first Jew the interest that he owes the non-Jew. The second Jew did not lend anything to the first Jew, but only to the non-Jew, and he merely stands in the non-Jew's place to receive the interest directly from the Jew. Tur and Rosh.

And according to the first view, etc. This is not comparable to the law above in seif 10, where if the Jew redeems the collateral it is forbidden. There, from the moment the Jew gives the collateral to the non-Jew and the non-Jew borrows upon it, it appears that he is borrowing for the Jew's benefit. Alternatively, there, since the non-Jew took the collateral from him against his will, the Jew certainly did not transfer ownership of it to him. Here, however, one can say that he did transfer ownership to him. So wrote the Beit Yosef regarding the law of seif 10. This also explains why there is no difficulty from seif 9 above, where it is forbidden when the lender knows that the collateral belongs to a Jew. There the non-Jew is borrowing for the Jew's benefit. The later authorities likewise write this.

segments_en: This is permitted. This applies not only where he lent him 100 to be repaid as 150, but even where he stipulated that he pay a specified amount of interest each month. Beit Yosef in the name of Sefer HaTerumah, cited by Darkei Moshe.

And some say that he is not, etc. The Beit Yosef writes that l'chatchila we rule that whenever the lender can first demand payment from the guarantor, the arrangement is forbidden unless the lender accepts upon himself not to demand payment from the guarantor until he first demands payment from the borrower and cannot collect from him, or the borrower is violent and the rabbinical court cannot extract payment from him, or he does not appear before the court, such as where he fled, and the like. Whenever the guarantor functions like an ordinary guarantor, it is permitted. B'dieved, however, we rely on the dissenting view, and where the money presently stands, we leave it in the possessor's hands in accordance with the rule in monetary doubts that the burden of proof rests upon the claimant. End of the Beit Yosef's words. It is clear from his words that with an unconditional guarantor who entirely replaces the borrower, even if he has already paid the interest, the money is extracted from the lender. This is unlike the view of the Rama in Darkei Moshe. The Bach is even more lenient and rules like R' Yosef Karkosa that the arrangement is forbidden only l'chatchila, but b'dieved the guarantor bears the entire loss since it resulted because of him, and there is no prohibition of interest even with such an unconditional guarantor. The view of all the other poskim is not so. It appears in my humble opinion that R' Yosef Karkosa himself was lenient only regarding an arev kablan, but not regarding a guarantor who entirely replaces the borrower. See there. This also resolves the difficulty left by Responsa Masas Binyamin at the end of siman 67 against R' Yosef Karkosa and the Rama, that the Gemara implies that where a Jew serves as guarantor the interest is forbidden by Torah law. One can say that the Gemara discusses an unconditional guarantor who entirely replaces the borrower. Even without this, there is no difficulty, because they may hold like the Baal HaItur, cited by the Beit Yosef, that the Gemara specifically discusses a non-Jew who borrowed from a Jew, etc. See there.

segments_en: One may fix a price with gleaners according to the gleaners' market price. Even Rambam, who was stringent above regarding old produce when there was no established price at all, agrees here that each class has its own established price. Above, both were the same type of produce and were ultimately expected to reach the same price. Here, however, the distinction is that the gleaner's grain is a mixture of rye and wheat, which is effectively a different type from the householder's grain, and they will never have the same price. Each therefore has its own permanent established market price, and one may contract with each according to its own price.

But he may not fix a price with a householder. The Gemara explains that a gleaner, if he has no produce, can borrow from another gleaner, whereas if a householder has none, it is beneath his dignity to borrow from a gleaner. Alternatively, one who gives money to a householder gives it for superior produce. It appears that there is a practical difference between these two answers where the householder explicitly says,

segments_en: Also for himself, etc. He may do so with other money that is not partnership money, whether purchasing the same type of merchandise, and all the more so a different type. Beit Yosef and the later authorities. This is not comparable to the case above in seif 29 concerning a shop. In a shop he is obligated to remain there all day engaged in the partnership business and not neglect it for another business. Here that consideration does not apply. Prisha.

He should not sell them together, because perhaps the merchandise he purchased for himself is not as good as the partnership merchandise, and his partner would thereby suffer a loss. Beit Yosef and the later authorities. Where there is a doubt in the law or a dispute among the poskim whether a particular payment constitutes fixed interest or merely the semblance of interest, Responsa R' Aharon Sasson, siman 162, cites Maharam di Modena as ruling stringently because it is a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition. R' Aharon Sasson disagrees and holds that it is a monetary doubt, in which we rule leniently for the possessor because the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, unless the majority of poskim agree that it constitutes fixed interest. In that case it is a doubt concerning a Torah prohibition and we follow the majority. This likewise appears from the words of other later authorities. It appears to me that the rabbinical court should tell him that he is committing a prohibition and should warn him strongly, and he himself should certainly act stringently. But if he disregards all of this, the rabbinical court has no power to extract money from him, since the matter remains a doubt in the law. At first glance there is proof from what the Gemara states concerning gifts to kohanim, as explained above in siman 61, seif 23, and below concerning a firstborn animal in siman 305, seif 13, and in many other places, where the possessor is exempt because the burden of proof rests upon the claimant, even though a Torah-level positive commandment is involved. See below, siman 259, seif katan 14.
